citationText: 28. See Farnsworth P. T. , U.S. Patent No. 2,087,683: filed April 26, 1933, issued July 20, 1937. While this patent is titled an “Image Dissector,” it was not a cold cathode tube in which the entire image passed in front of a scanning aperture to create the picture signal. It described a very advanced storage-type camera tube that used a low-velocity scanning beam from a hot cathode. It used the beam to explore a target made up of a large number of insulated areas, or “islands,” of photoelectric active material. It was planned to have the beam touch the target lightly and restore the electrons lost due to photoelectric emission. The modulated beam was to return to an anode, where its output became the picture signal. While there is no proof that Philo Farnsworth ever did build a tube of this type, its features were later incorporated by Harley Iams and Albert Rose into the RCA Orthicon and Image Orthicon camera tubes that made postwar television possible. Farnsworth's patent was so powerful that it dominated the field. This was one of Farnsworth's greatest triumphs.
